<reason>B won by consistently distinguishing effective policing from the additional value of broader legal powers. A offered a plausible prevention mechanism, concrete safeguards, and an honest concession about withdrawing ineffective tactics. But B showed that those safeguards either resembled existing individualized suspicion or still permitted searches based principally on proximity. More decisively, A repeatedly treated its possible benefits as concrete while dismissing possible safety costs as reversible friction. B answered both pressure questions directly and explained why lost cooperation and diverted investigative effort undermine that asymmetry.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest rebuttal was that oversight can reverse a policy but cannot reverse violence resulting from lost warnings or displaced investigative work. Combined with A’s concession that increased seizures need not mean fewer stabbings, this defeated A’s central comparison of corrigible inconvenience against irreversible death.</best_rebuttal>
